findings.title: Database write hidden inside validator via BlockedEmail.should_block?
findings.body: EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?(value), which performs a write (increments match_count, sets last_match_at, calls record.save) as a side effect. Validators must be pure: this implementation causes an extra UPDATE on the blocked_emails table on every User validation. match_count is therefore inflated by every call to user.valid?, every save attempt (and the create flow calls valid? then save, so it is double-counted), admin edits in the console, test suites, and any code that calls .valid? on a User collection. Move the match-counting side effect out of the validator — e.g., call an explicit record_blocked_attempt! from UsersController#create after the block decision — and leave should_block? read-only.

findings.title: Lost-update race on match_count / last_match_at
findings.body: Lines 14–16 do a non-atomic read-modify-write: `record.match_count += 1` mutates the in-memory AR object, then `record.save` writes the row. Two concurrent signups for the same blocked email can both SELECT match_count=N, both compute N+1, and the second save overwrites the first, losing one increment (and possibly a concurrent last_match_at update). Replace this with a single atomic SQL statement, e.g.: `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` so the increment and timestamp happen in one statement that the database serializes.

findings.title: EmailValidator spec only covers the BlockedEmail branch
findings.body: The spec stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never exercises the whitelist/blacklist code paths. It does not verify: (a) an email matching SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist is accepted, (b) an email not matching the whitelist is rejected with user.email.not_allowed, (c) an email matching SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist is rejected, (d) the precedence rule (whitelist takes priority over blacklist), or (e) the early-exit when record.errors[attribute] is already populated by an earlier validator. These are real production code paths and need direct coverage.

findings.title: should_block? is misnamed — it has side effects
findings.body: The method name should_block? reads as a pure predicate ('does this email get blocked?'), but the implementation performs a database write whenever a matching record is found. Any caller that reasonably expects a read-only check — including future code, integration tests, or the EmailValidator itself — will be surprised by writes. Either rename to make the side effect explicit (e.g., record_match_and_should_block!) or split responsibilities: keep should_block? as a pure lookup and add a separate record_match! that the caller invokes only when it actually wants to count the attempt.
